title: Big-O Upper Bound Definition
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: f(n) = O(g(n)) means there are constants c > 0 and n0 such that 0 <= f(n) <= c g(n) for all n >= n0.
short: Eventually f grows no faster than a constant multiple of g.
long: Eventually f grows no faster than a constant multiple of g. Big-O gives an asymptotic upper bound and is the standard language for worst-case running times.
proof: Given witnesses c and n0, the inequality holds for every larger n by definition.
consequence: It suppresses machine constants and low-order terms so algorithms can be compared structurally.

title: Big-Omega and Big-Theta Bounds
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: f(n) = Omega(g(n)) means g(n) = O(f(n)), and f(n) = Theta(g(n)) means both f = O(g) and f = Omega(g).
short: Theta pins the growth rate from both sides.
long: Theta pins the growth rate from both sides. Saying an algorithm is Theta(n log n) is stronger than saying it is O(n^2).
proof: Combining the two sets of witnesses c1 and c2 gives the two-sided inequality for large n.
consequence: Theta notation expresses tight bounds such as the exact order of merge sort.

title: Little-o and Strict Asymptotic Dominance
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: f(n) = o(g(n)) means f(n)/g(n) tends to zero, so g grows strictly faster than f.
short: The ratio vanishes rather than staying bounded.
long: The ratio vanishes rather than staying bounded. For example log n = o(n^epsilon) for every epsilon > 0.
proof: The limit definition is equivalent to f(n) <= epsilon g(n) eventually for every epsilon > 0.
consequence: It distinguishes tight Theta bounds from strictly weaker upper bounds.

title: Worst, Average and Amortised Costs
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Worst-case cost maximises over inputs, average-case cost averages over an input distribution, and amortised cost averages over a sequence of operations.
short: Three different ways to summarise a running time.
long: Three different ways to summarise a running time. An O(1) amortised bound can hide an O(n) single operation; an average-case bound depends on a distributional assumption.
proof: The three quantities are defined by different aggregations of the same per-operation or per-input cost.
consequence: Stating which notion is meant prevents misinterpretation of algorithmic guarantees.

title: Unit-Cost RAM Model
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: The RAM model assumes a sequential machine in which each arithmetic, comparison and memory access takes one time unit.
short: Count operations, not machine cycles.
long: Count operations, not machine cycles. It ignores caches, pipelining and word-size overflow, making analysis tractable.
proof: The model is a definition: each primitive instruction is charged unit cost.
consequence: Most textbook O-notation bounds are stated in this model.

title: Word RAM and Transdichotomous Model
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: The word RAM allows constant-time operations on w-bit words with w at least log n, so an entire input index fits in one word.
short: Words scale with problem size.
long: Words scale with problem size. It enables bit-parallel tricks and integer sorting bounds unavailable in the comparison model.
proof: Setting word size proportional to log n lets the machine address any input location and pack log n bits.
consequence: It is the standard theoretical model for integer algorithms and succinct data structures.

title: Bit Complexity versus Arithmetic Complexity
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Treating arithmetic as unit-cost can hide the bit operations needed for large numbers; multiplying two n-bit integers costs O(n^2) naively.
short: Big integers make constant-time arithmetic inaccurate.
long: Big integers make constant-time arithmetic inaccurate. Fast multiplication algorithms reduce this, but the distinction remains important in cryptography and exact computation.
proof: Schoolbook multiplication forms n^2 partial products of single bits.
consequence: Bit complexity is the right model when operands grow with the input size.

title: Aggregate Method of Amortised Analysis
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: The aggregate method bounds the total cost of m operations directly and divides by m to obtain the amortised cost per operation.
short: Prove a total bound, then average.
long: Prove a total bound, then average. It works best when operations are similar, as with dynamic-array resizing.
proof: If the total cost of any m operations is O(mg(n)), the average cost is O(g(n)).
consequence: It is the simplest of the three standard amortised-analysis methods.

title: Accounting Method of Amortised Analysis
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: The accounting method charges each operation a fixed fee, storing surplus credit on objects to pay for later expensive operations.
short: Overcharge cheap operations to fund rare costly ones.
long: Overcharge cheap operations to fund rare costly ones. The credit invariant must hold after every operation.
proof: If total charged fees are an upper bound on total actual cost and credit never goes negative, the amortised bound follows.
consequence: It gives an intuitive proof of amortised O(1) for push and pop with multipop.

title: Potential Method of Amortised Analysis
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: The potential method defines a nonnegative function Phi on states and charges operation i the actual cost plus Phi(state_i) - Phi(state_{i-1}).
short: Stored potential pays for future work.
long: Stored potential pays for future work. Because the potential telescopes, the total amortised cost exceeds the total actual cost by at most the initial potential.
proof: Summing the charges gives sum c_i + Phi_m - Phi_0, which is at least sum c_i when Phi_0 = 0 and Phi_m >= 0.
consequence: Potentials handle complex structures such as splay trees and Fibonacci heaps.

title: Multipop Stack Amortised Bound
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: A stack supporting push, pop and multipop(k) in which multipop removes up to k elements has O(1) amortised cost per operation when the potential is the stack size.
short: A multipop pays for itself by releasing stored potential.
long: A multipop pays for itself by releasing stored potential. A multipop can cost O(n) in one step but decreases the potential by the same amount.
proof: Amortised cost of multipop is k + (-k) = O(1), while push costs 1 + 1 and pop costs 1 - 1.
consequence: It is the canonical first example of the potential method.

title: Substitution Method for Recurrences
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: The substitution method guesses a bound on T(n) and verifies it by induction, possibly subtracting a lower-order term to make the induction go through.
short: Guess, then prove by induction.
long: Guess, then prove by induction. Changing variables can handle recurrences with floors and ceilings.
proof: Assume the bound for smaller arguments, substitute into the recurrence and confirm it for n.
consequence: It proves bounds for recurrences not covered by standard templates.

title: Recursion Tree Method
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Drawing a recursion tree and summing work level by level converts divide-and-conquer recurrences into geometric or arithmetic sums.
short: Add up the cost at each depth.
long: Add up the cost at each depth. It gives intuition even when a formal induction is still needed to confirm the bound.
proof: Each node's cost is the nonrecursive work for its subproblem; summing over all nodes at a level and over levels yields T(n).
consequence: It explains why the shape of f(n) determines the asymptotic solution.

title: Work Accumulation Across Recursive Levels
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: For T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n), the total cost is governed by whether f decreases, stays level with, or grows relative to n^{log_b a} across levels.
short: Leaf count versus per-level cost decides the winner.
long: Leaf count versus per-level cost decides the winner. This is the mechanism behind the three common cases of divide-and-conquer recurrences.
proof: At level i there are a^i subproblems of size n/b^i, so per-level work is a^i f(n/b^i) and the sequence is compared with a geometric progression.
consequence: It builds intuition for recurrence-solving theorems without memorising their statements.

title: Akra–Bazzi General Recurrence Method
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: For T(n) = sum_i a_i T(b_i n) + g(n) with a_i > 0 and 0 < b_i < 1, the solution is Theta(n^p (1 + integral of g(u)/u^{p+1})), where sum_i a_i b_i^p = 1.
short: One exponent p captures arbitrarily uneven splits.
long: One exponent p captures arbitrarily uneven splits. It generalises the standard equal-split recurrence theorem to multiple unequal subproblems.
proof: A change of variables to logarithmic scale turns the recurrence into a renewal equation whose characteristic exponent is p.
consequence: It resolves recurrences from algorithms with unbalanced partition sizes.

title: Dynamic Programming Optimal Substructure
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: A problem has optimal substructure when an optimal solution contains optimal solutions to its subproblems.
short: Optimal answers can be assembled from optimal smaller answers.
long: Optimal answers can be assembled from optimal smaller answers. It is one of the two hallmarks of dynamic programming, alongside overlapping subproblems.
proof: If a sub-solution could be improved while keeping the rest fixed, the whole solution would improve, contradicting optimality.
consequence: It justifies Bellman equations and bottom-up DP recurrences.

title: Memoisation versus Tabulation
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Memoisation caches results of recursive calls on demand, while tabulation fills a table bottom-up in dependency order.
short: Top-down caching versus bottom-up iteration.
long: Top-down caching versus bottom-up iteration. Both achieve one computation per distinct subproblem; tabulation avoids recursion overhead and controls space.
proof: Each memoised call computes a state once, as does each table entry filled in order.
consequence: The choice affects stack depth, cache behaviour and ease of state compression.

title: Overlapping Subproblems Criterion
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: A recursive algorithm has overlapping subproblems when the same subproblem is solved repeatedly, making caching worthwhile.
short: DP wins when recursion re-solves the same work.
long: DP wins when recursion re-solves the same work. Quicksort has disjoint subproblems and gains nothing from memoisation; Fibonacci recursion has heavy overlap.
proof: If the recursion tree has repeated nodes, storing results replaces repeated subtrees by table lookups.
consequence: It distinguishes dynamic programming from ordinary divide and conquer.

title: Greedy Choice Property
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: A problem has the greedy choice property if some optimal solution begins with the locally best choice.
short: A myopic first move can be provably safe.
long: A myopic first move can be provably safe. It must be established for each problem; greedy algorithms fail without it.
proof: An exchange argument transforms an optimal solution into one making the greedy choice without increasing cost.
consequence: It underlies Huffman coding, interval scheduling and MST algorithms.

title: Exchange Arguments for Greedy Correctness
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: An exchange argument shows a greedy choice is safe by modifying any optimal solution to include it without worsening the objective.
short: Convert the best solution into one agreeing with greedy.
long: Convert the best solution into one agreeing with greedy. The technique appears in proofs of Kruskal, Prim, Huffman and interval scheduling.
proof: Locate the greedy element in the optimal solution's structure, swap it in and verify constraints and cost.
consequence: It is the workhorse proof technique for greedy optimality.

title: Matroid Greedy Optimality
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: For a weighted matroid, sorting elements by decreasing weight and adding each feasible element yields a maximum-weight independent set.
short: Matroid axioms are exactly what greedy needs.
long: Matroid axioms are exactly what greedy needs. Graphic matroids explain why Kruskal works; partition matroids model scheduling constraints.
proof: The exchange axiom lets any optimal basis be transformed to include the greedy prefix by induction.
consequence: It gives a uniform proof of many seemingly unrelated greedy algorithms.

title: Greedy Fails for 0/1 Knapsack
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: Picking items by value-to-weight ratio can be suboptimal when items cannot be split.
short: Indivisibility breaks the ratio argument.
long: Indivisibility breaks the ratio argument. With capacity 50 and items (10,60), (20,100) and (30,120), greedy by ratio takes the first two for 160, while the last two give 220.
proof: The ratio order fills capacity with high-density items but leaves unusable space; no exchange argument can force the optimal pair to be chosen.
consequence: Use dynamic programming for 0/1 knapsack and greedy only for the fractional version.

title: 0/1 Knapsack Dynamic Program
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: For n items and integer capacity W, DP over items and capacity solves 0/1 knapsack in O(nW) time and O(W) space with a rolling array.
short: Decide each item once against every reachable capacity.
long: Decide each item once against every reachable capacity. The bound is pseudopolynomial because W is a number, not the count of input bits.
proof: After processing item i, dp[w] stores the best value using a subset of the first i items with weight at most w.
consequence: It is the standard pseudo-polynomial algorithm for a fundamental NP-hard problem.

title: Fractional Knapsack Greedy Ratio
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: When items are divisible, sorting by value per unit weight and taking as much as possible gives an optimal solution in O(n log n).
short: Spend capacity on the best value per pound first.
long: Spend capacity on the best value per pound first. The final item may be taken partially, which is precisely why greedy is valid here.
proof: If a cheaper-per-unit item is taken while a dearer one remains, swapping mass increases value until no such inversion exists.
consequence: It contrasts with the 0/1 case and illustrates when greedy is exact.

title: Longest Common Subsequence DP
subject: Algorithm Analysis
statement: The length of the longest common subsequence of strings of lengths n and m follows from a recurrence that either matches the last characters or discards one, computable in O(nm) time.
short: Build the answer from prefixes of both strings.
long: Build the answer from prefixes of both strings. Space can be reduced to O(min(n,m)) if only the length is needed.
proof: If the last characters match they can be used, otherwise at least one last character is discarded; the recurrence considers both cases.
consequence: It is a canonical DP template with applications in diff tools and bioinformatics.
